The Rise of Weather Wimpiness

Floyd is making me reconsider my belief in a Divine Power—perhaps not because of the storm itself, but because of how we now react to it. Since I recently confessed to you my growing skepticism that modern acts of God are invariably overblown, this one has been hurtling straight toward metropolitan New York—toward me, I suspect—serving as a kind of cosmic rebuke to my own youthful arrogance. This morning, the kids’ school canceled classes at 6:45, prompting me to quietly contemplate backing out of a book-reading and signing I’m scheduled for tonight. I can’t help but think people today are far more weather-averse than we were as children. (Canceling school for rain?) I grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where weather wimpiness was practically inconceivable. Extreme weather wasn’t just common there—it was the thrill of life. (And, briefly, the brief, chilling presence of Charles Starkweather, the real-life serial killer portrayed by Martin Sheen in *Badlands*, when I was four.) The one time a tornado actually touched down in our yard—small, but undeniable—I was away at summer camp. I’ve never regretted missing anything more.

Such studies
        can also reveal a lot about the general role of microevolution in species divergence.
        Reinforcement provides a pathway toward the completion of the speciation process.
        Imagine that two divergent populations (potentially even classified as separate species)
        come into contact after a period of allopatry (Figure 1). If the populations have been
        apart for a long time, evolved differences between them will cause a certain degree of
        incompatibility when the populations come together. Often, this incompatibility comes in
        the form of low hybrid fitness (postzygotic isolation) or mismatched mating characteristics
        (premating isolation). The degree of the development of these isolating mechanisms is
        roughly proportional to the genetic distance between the populations, reflecting the fact
        that incompatibilities accumulate over time (Coyne and Orr 1989).
        If the isolating mechanisms between these populations are only partially complete,
        extensive hybridization may occur. This can result in fusion back into a single population,
        or in the swamping of one population's gene pool by the genes of the other (extinction).

Slate’s Jacob Weisberg weighed in, calling McCain’s performance courageous, Bush’s effective, yet also evasive. Separately, Wen Ho Lee, an engineer at the Los Alamos, N.M., weapons lab, pleaded not guilty to 59 counts of removing classified data from his computer, with the indictment alleging he did so with the intent to injure the United States and to secure an advantage for a foreign power—though he was not charged with the more serious crime of spying. Asian-American activists denounced the case, calling Lee a "sacrificial lamb" singled out because of his race, while the Justice Department maintained he remains a security threat, possibly having "alter[ed] the global balance of nuclear arms." Critics countered that the threat would never have reached such proportions had the Clinton administration not flubbed the investigation, a point Slate had outlined in August.
